column2: A nuclear sub has gone missing. Men are trapped, and time is running out. How can we possibly find them in time?
Start with a strange idea. A search that finds nothing has still told you something.
This happened. In May of nineteen sixty-eight the U S S Scorpion, a nuclear submarine, was heading home across the Atlantic with ninety-nine men aboard.
She was due at Norfolk, Virginia, on the twenty-seventh, and did not arrive. For nine days the Navy searched the ocean, as if her crew might still be saved.
They could not be. She had gone down five days before she was due, in water about two miles deep. All ninety-nine men were lost.
Nobody knew that yet. And even to find the wreck, the Navy faced the first question of any search. Where do you look?

Not everywhere. Sound recordings had narrowed the search to a patch of sea twelve miles on a side. But the sled that carried the search gear saw a strip only two hundred feet wide. One pass over the whole patch meant forty-six hundred miles of towing. By the end of October it had managed a thousand.
So where would you look first?
The natural answer is, wherever she most likely is. So you need a map of how likely each place is.
Start small. A sea of four cells, and two stories of what might have happened.
In the first story she held her course. Then she is probably in cell A, maybe in B, less likely in C.
In the second, something turned her, and she could be anywhere.
People who know submarines weigh the stories. Say sixty to forty. Now picture a hundred dots, sixty from the first story and forty from the second. Each dot is one place she could be.
The first story puts half of its dots in cell A. The second puts a quarter of its dots there. What is the chance she is in cell A?
Half of sixty is thirty. A quarter of forty is ten. Forty dots in a hundred. Forty percent.
Count every cell that way and you have the map. Forty, thirty, twenty, ten.

The Navy's map was made the same way. In July, John Craven, who led the search's technical advisers, and a colleague named Andrews set out nine stories of how the Scorpion might have been lost, and gave each a weight.
A mathematician, Henry Richardson, had a computer play those stories out ten thousand times. Ten thousand dots.
Then he counted the dots in every cell. This is the map they printed.
One cell stands out, with one dot in every eight. They called it E five. Was she there?
Almost. The wreck lay in a neighbouring cell, two hundred and sixty yards from the edge of E five.
But the map alone did not find her. It took five months, and a method for using a map like this.
Back to the small sea. Forty percent says search cell A first. But a search is not a sure thing.
Cell A is a canyon. A search there sees the wreck only one time in four. In the flat cells, a search sees it two times in three.
So ask a better question. How likely is one search of a cell to find her? For that, she has to be there, and the search has to see her.
Forty percent, seen one time in four. Thirty percent, seen two times in three. Which cell gives the better chance of a find, A or B?
Cell B. A quarter of forty is ten. Two thirds of thirty is twenty. Twice the chance.
The chance of a find is the chance she is there, times the chance of seeing her. So the best cell to search is not always the likeliest.
So we search cell B. And the search comes back empty.
That is not nothing. Look at the dots. Thirty are in B, and this search would have found two out of three of them. Twenty dots.
If she were at any of those twenty, we would have her. We do not. So they go out.
Eighty dots are left, and she is at one of them. Ten are still in B, because a search can miss.
Ten dots out of eighty. What is the chance she is in cell B now?
One in eight. Twelve and a half percent, down from thirty.
Now look at cell A. Nobody searched it, and it has the same forty dots. But forty out of eighty is one half. Searching B made A more likely.
Every cell we did not search went up, by the same factor.
That move has a name. Bayes' rule, after Thomas Bayes, an English minister who died in seventeen sixty-one.
In words. Take each cell's chance. Multiply by the chance that the search would come back empty if she were there. Then scale the whole map so it adds up to a hundred again.
The cell you searched drops. Every other cell rises. And the map is ready for the next search.
Here is the new map. Cell A has half the chance now. But A is the canyon. Where do you search next?
Cell C. A half, seen one time in four, is twelve and a half percent. A quarter, seen two times in three, is nearly seventeen.
Search. Come back empty. Update. Choose again. That loop is the whole method.
Always search where the next search is most likely to find her. Is that really the best you can do?
Yes. For a wreck that stays put, and searches that cost the same, it is a theorem, proved in nineteen sixty-seven. No other order of searches is ever ahead.
On the Navy's map, the difference is large. Suppose every search sees a wreck in its cell two times in three. One plan sweeps the grid row by row. The other follows the rule.
After twenty searches, the sweep has had less than one chance in a hundred of finding her. The rule, better than one in two.
The rule reaches the wreck's own cell on its thirty-fifth search. The sweep, on its eighty-first.
Why would a search see a wreck only two times in three? The answer comes from the Second World War.
Hunting submarines, a group of American scientists, Bernard Koopman among them, asked how much of an area a searcher really covers.

With perfect lanes, side by side, enough track to pass over a cell once would cover all of it. But at sea your lanes land where they land. Some overlap, some leave gaps, and on average the same track covers sixty-three percent.
Koopman's formula gives that number, and the next ones. Twice the track, eighty-six percent. Three times, ninety-five. Each pass finds less than the one before.
So take a search that sees two times in three, and run it twice over the same cell. What is the chance that at least one pass sees her?
Eight in nine. The first pass leaves a third unseen, and the second finds two thirds of that. No number of passes makes it certain.
A wreck stays where it is. A person in the water does not. Wind and current carry them, and nobody knows either one exactly.
So every dot moves with its own guess at the wind and the current. The map drifts, and it spreads.
And a person is hard to see. From a helicopter, the Coast Guard counts on spotting someone in the water within a strip only a tenth of a mile wide.
Let the cloud's radius double, and fly the same length of track. What happens to the coverage?
It falls to a quarter. Twice the radius is four times the area.
In this model, a flight that would find the person ninety-three times in a hundred after one hour finds them thirteen times in a hundred after twelve. That is why hours matter.

The United States Coast Guard has searched this way since nineteen seventy-four. Its software moves thousands of dots, each a possible drifting person or boat, and updates them by Bayes' rule after every empty search.
In July of twenty thirteen, a lobsterman named John Aldridge fell off his boat at night, about forty miles off Long Island. Nobody saw him go.
The searchers had to guess when he fell, and guessed the evening before. So the first map put its dots almost thirty miles too far north.
The map was wrong because its story was wrong. What could fix it?
Evidence. On deck, his partner found an open hatch and pumps running, work Aldridge would not have started until far offshore. He had fallen hours later.
The Coast Guard ran the map again, and the dots moved south. That afternoon a helicopter flying through them spotted him, alive, after almost twelve hours in the water.
June, two thousand nine. Air France flight four four seven, from Rio to Paris, was lost over the Atlantic with two hundred and twenty-eight people aboard.
The wreck had to lie inside a circle forty nautical miles in radius. Ships and sonar searched it for nearly two years, and did not find it.
Then a team of search analysts built a map from three ingredients, weighted thirty-five, thirty-five and thirty, and folded in every empty search.
One search needed a decision. For a month, ships had listened for the beacons on the flight recorders, and heard nothing. How much should that silence count?
If the beacons worked, a great deal. If they were broken, not at all. So the analysts drew the map twice, once counting the silence, and once leaving it out.
The search resumed near the centre of the circle and found the wreck within a week. It lay in a high-chance part of the second map, in water the listening ships had already crossed.
The same thing had happened in nineteen sixty-eight. The Navy's map reached the search ship in August, two months into the search. From then on, every pass of the sled was scored, cell by cell.
By October, the ship's numbers said one cell had been searched ninety-four percent thoroughly. Of every hundred dots there, ninety-four went out. It was the cell with the wreck in it.
The wreck was there, and the sled had been over that water. What went wrong?

The estimate of how well they were looking. At sea, the sonar was credited with a strip eight hundred feet wide. Measured afterwards against the wreck itself, it got zero, and the camera and the magnetometer about two hundred feet each. The honest figure for that cell was sixty-five percent.
She was found on the twenty-eighth of October, when the sled went back to a scrap of metal photographed that summer, in a part of the map that had been likely from the start.
An empty search only tells you something if it could have found what you were looking for.
Four searches, each against its map.
Palomares, nineteen sixty-six. A hydrogen bomb, lost in the sea off Spain. Craven first weighed stories there. The bomb itself was found where a fisherman had watched it fall.
Scorpion. Beside the map's top cell, in a cell the numbers had nearly written off.
Air France. In a high-chance part of the second map, the one that set the silence aside.
John Aldridge. Inside the dots, once the story was put right.
Three of those maps had something wrong in them at first. A strip too wide. A silence trusted too far. A story five hours off. So why does the method work?
Because it never needs the first map to be right. It needs you to say what you believe, to say honestly how well you looked, and to let every empty search move the dots.
The ninety-nine men of the Scorpion could not be saved. The method that searched for them now searches for people who can.
